mcqs.question: What specifically does dropout prevent units in a layer from doing?
options: Using more than one activation function
Co-adapting — relying on a narrow, brittle combination of specific other units
mcqs.explanation: By randomly zeroing different units each step, dropout stops units from depending on always having the same specific neighbors active, which forces more robust, individually useful features. Units still learn and still receive gradients — dropout doesn't disable learning, it changes what gets learned.

mcqs.question: During training, validation loss bottoms out at epoch 12 and starts rising afterward while training loss keeps falling. What does early stopping do here?
options: Stops training and keeps the checkpoint from around epoch 12, before validation loss started rising
Continues training to the final epoch, then keeps the last checkpoint
Restarts training from scratch with a different architecture
Ignores validation loss entirely and only tracks training loss
mcqs.explanation: Early stopping tracks validation loss specifically because it's the signal for when the model starts overfitting training-set noise; it keeps the best checkpoint (around epoch 12 here) rather than a later, more-overfit one. Training loss alone can't reveal overfitting since it keeps improving even as generalization worsens.

mcqs.question: A deployed model with dropout layers gives a different prediction for the identical input on two separate API calls. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model wasn't trained long enough
Dropout was left active at inference instead of being disabled
The learning rate was too high during training
mcqs.explanation: Dropout randomly zeroes units on each forward pass; if it's still active at inference (model not switched to eval mode), identical inputs will produce different outputs across calls, since a different random set of units gets dropped each time. The other options would cause consistent but poor predictions, not non-determinism.
